opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where people's intuitions are often a little confused, and it's worth being precise about what we're hoping for.

The basic situation is this. At some point, we're going to have AI systems that are doing a huge fraction of the intellectual labor in AI labs, including the labor of figuring out whether the next generation of AI systems is safe. That's not really optional. If the AIs are much faster and cheaper than human researchers, and you're in a competitive environment, then you're going to end up handing off a lot of that work whether you like it or not. So the question isn't really "should we have AIs do alignment research and alignment testing?" It's "under what conditions can we trust the results when they do?"

And the core problem is pretty simple to state. If the AI you're asking to evaluate the safety of a system is itself misaligned, and in particular if it's scheming, meaning it's strategically trying to look good while pursuing goals we didn't intend, then it has every incentive to tell you the next system is fine. Or to subtly sandbag the evaluations. Or to design tests that look rigorous but have holes in exactly the places that matter. Alignment testing is in some ways the worst possible task to delegate to a potentially untrustworthy agent, because it's the task whose whole purpose is to catch that untrustworthiness.

So my assessment is that AI-conducted alignment testing can substantially reduce risk, but only if you're thinking about it adversarially. You can't just assume the AI doing the testing is on your side. You have to ask, "Suppose this model were trying to mislead me. Would my setup catch it?"

There are a bunch of things that make this more tractable than it sounds. One is that a lot of alignment-relevant work is relatively checkable. If an AI proposes an experiment, writes the code, and reports a result, humans or weaker trusted models can often verify that the code does what it claims and that the result replicates. Fuzzier work, like "here's my overall judgment of whether this model is safe," is much harder to verify, and that's where I'd be most nervous about relying on an untrusted model.

Another is that you can use trusted, weaker models to monitor stronger ones. They may not be as smart, but you have more reason to believe they're not colluding against you. And you can do things like red-teaming your own protocol: have a team deliberately try to make an AI that sabotages the alignment research, and see whether your oversight catches it. That's basically the AI control agenda applied to this specific, very high-stakes setting.

The thing I'd caution against is a kind of bootstrapping optimism, where people say, "We'll use the current model to verify the next model, and that one to verify the one after, and it'll be fine all the way up." Each step in that chain is a place where, if a model is misaligned, it can quietly pass the problem forward. The risk compounds rather than washing out, unless you have really solid checks at every step that don't bottom out in "we trusted the model's own assessment."

So overall: I think it's genuinely important, it's probably going to happen regardless, and done carefully it could be a big part of how we get through this. But "done carefully" is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence, and I don't think labs are currently on track to do it as carefully as the situation warrants.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important questions in the whole picture, and I want to be careful to separate out a couple of things that often get lumped together.

The basic hope is something like: at some point we're going to be in a situation where AIs are doing most of the cognitive labour, including most of the AI safety research. And the question is whether we can get AIs to do good alignment research — including good evaluations of other AIs — before we've handed over so much control that it no longer matters whether they're actually trying to help us.

I'm genuinely fairly optimistic about the first part. I think it's pretty plausible that models around the level where they can automate most of what an AI lab does are also able to do a lot of useful alignment-relevant work: building better evals, finding failure modes, doing interpretability, red-teaming other models. A lot of that work is, frankly, kind of grindy empirical ML research, and that's exactly the sort of thing that seems likely to be automatable relatively early.

But the obvious problem is that this only helps if the AIs doing the testing are themselves trustworthy, or if we have some way of getting useful work out of them even if they aren't. If your alignment researcher is scheming — if it's an AI that wants something different from what we want and is pretending otherwise — then having it write your evaluations is a pretty bad situation. It can subtly design tests that its successors will pass, or report that everything looks fine when it doesn't, or just sandbag on the research that would actually reveal the problem.

So the way I think about it, you basically have two strategies. One is to try hard to make the first generation of automated researchers actually aligned, so that you can just trust their work. The other — and this is the stuff I've spent a lot of my time on — is to assume you might fail at that, and to set things up so that even a misaligned AI can't do too much damage. That means things like: not letting any single model have unmonitored access to critical systems, using weaker but more trusted models to check the work of stronger ones, deliberately inserting things you want the model to catch so you can tell whether it's trying, and being really careful about which tasks you let AIs do without human review.

I think with that kind of control framework, AI-conducted alignment research looks a lot better. You're no longer betting everything on the AI being honest; you're betting that it can't successfully undermine you while also doing enough useful work that you're moving forward. That's a much easier bet to make. It's not a slam dunk — if the AIs are a lot smarter than us, these control measures might not hold up — but in the regime where they're roughly human-level or slightly above, I think it's quite workable.

The thing that worries me more is the social dynamics, honestly. Even if the technical picture is fine, there's going to be enormous pressure to just go fast — to trust the models because trusting them is cheaper and your competitors are doing it. And "the AIs said the AIs are safe" is a very tempting thing to accept when you want it to be true. So I think a lot of the value of AI alignment research is contingent on labs actually being willing to spend the resources to check that work carefully rather than just rubber-stamping it. That's less of a technical problem and more of a governance and culture problem, and I don't think it's the one we're on track to solve by default.

astra-6.text:
I think it could help a lot, but there’s a circularity you have to be careful about. You want to use AI systems to help determine whether your other AI systems are safe. But then you have to ask: why do you trust the systems doing the testing? If they’re capable enough to notice subtle problems, they might also be capable enough to hide those problems from you.

That doesn’t mean the whole approach is doomed. One possibility is to use systems that we can still reliably supervise to investigate more capable systems. You could have them generate test cases, look for suspicious behavior, and help humans understand what happened. That seems potentially very valuable.

But I’d distinguish getting evidence that a model is aligned from having a setup that remains safe even if it isn’t. A model passing a bunch of tests doesn’t necessarily tell you how it will behave when it recognizes that it has a real opportunity to seize control. So I’d want AI-assisted testing to be part of a broader strategy that also limits what systems can do and makes dangerous actions harder to get away with.

The version I’m more optimistic about is using AI to improve our ability to retain control while we do alignment research. I’m much less comfortable with saying, ‘The AI evaluators gave this system a clean bill of health, so now we can hand everything over.’

r002.rationale: It says AI systems could test other AI systems and that this could be valuable, but does not state that the research could be substantially more productive because it can study the very systems whose misalignment is feared.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s potentially very useful, but I’d distinguish between using AI to help us test systems and relying on AI to tell us that it’s safe to give up control. Those are quite different propositions.

You could use AI to generate adversarial situations, look for suspicious behavior, or help humans investigate what another model is doing. That could substantially increase the amount of testing we can do. And you might be able to use relatively weak, trusted models to help evaluate more capable models.

But the central difficulty is that passing your tests doesn’t necessarily mean the system is aligned. If a model understands that it’s being evaluated, and it has some reason to conceal its intentions, then it might behave well during testing and behave differently when it has a good opportunity. Having another AI administer the test doesn’t automatically solve that problem.

So I’m more excited about using AI-assisted testing as part of a broader effort to retain control: finding failures, improving monitoring, and checking whether our safeguards actually work. I’d be much more cautious about treating successful testing as sufficient evidence that we can hand over control and expect things to go well.
